entries.note: Remote launching is deliberately outside this contract. The consumers' own scripts do it and hold knowledge that does not belong in an orchestrator: an SSH logon session has no window station, so a GL context cannot be created and the launch has to go through Task Scheduler with /IT; APK freshness is compared against the installed base.apk mtime. So the refusal is computed here, where the declaration is in hand, and names the project's own script actions bound to that device — derived from data, so rEngine still names no specific script. The string is carried on the config so the worker can refuse before anything reaches the retained host (the KI-043 lesson) and Games.start can refuse again for a direct caller, without two copies of the wording.

entries.note: Preflight is exported as a free function taking the root record, not a Games method, because it reads only the declaration, the filesystem and root.id/root.path — no session, surface or store state. That is what lets the replaceable workspace worker answer GET /api/game-config from its own checkout above a retained session host that predates contract 3, exactly as dashboard.mjs is already consumed from both processes. Games.inspect is now a one-line delegation, so the host and the worker run the same body and there is no second copy of the checks to drift. Launch stays a method: it needs Sessions and Surfaces, which are the host's process state. One consequence worth knowing: a bare executable candidate resolves through the calling process's PATH, so it is the worker's environment that answers when the worker serves the route. Contract 4 adds an options argument threaded to deviceStatus so an explicit refresh reaches the probe cache; it stays a free function for the same reason, since a probe needs only the root record and the shell environment.

THE rule of spec 082: a target bound to a non-local device is never resolved or stat-ed against the local filesystem. That check is exactly what produced "Game executable not found; expected build/vtmb-vr ..." for a target that is condition = "windows" and can never be built on the machine the workspace runs on — every word true, and the conclusion (build it) impossible. The cwd is skipped for the same reason: it is a directory on that machine. The record's own requires are still checked locally, because requires is local by definition even on a remote device. The regression test proves the rule rather than the symptom: it places the executable ON the local disk and asserts it is still unresolved, so the test cannot pass by the file merely being absent.

Preflight (inspectGame, above) reads the project's own declaration: the selected record is the one whose id matches gameId, or the first declared game when it is omitted; executable candidates resolve in order (absolute, root-relative with a Windows .exe fallback, bare name through the sidecar PATH), each declared requires file is stat'ed without symlink confinement so shared data can be linked in, as the qualification fixtures do, and a declared cwd must be an existing directory; nothing runs. embedded reserves a surface item and injects the macOS adapter (the qualified SDL interposition path); external spawns the plain PTY child so an SDL3/static application opens its own window and only its output is retained. Declared env is layered under the reservation and the adapter, and the reader already rejects RENGINE_/DYLD_/LD_ keys. Windows launch remains an explicit unsupported-integration error until the cooperative surface is wired and proven in that host.

entries.note: A launch is identified by root AND declared game id, not by root alone: contract 3 lets one project declare several games, and the owner's shape is that they run side by side (a flat target and a VR target at once). So concurrent requests coalesce per pair and a reuse only returns a running session whose game id matches. The preflight runs before the coalescing key exists because the key needs the resolved id, which also makes an unknown gameId a 404 rather than a silent default. An undeclared project fails before the reuse lookup so a game session started outside a declaration can never be handed back as "the project's game". The 2026-09-06 owner decision keeps that key when two dashboard actions name the same record with different argv: the declared id stays the single identity of a running game session (launch_game/game_preflight select by it, the snapshot carries it, the native tab binding and RENGINE_INITIAL_GAME resolve through it), so a differing launch is refused with both argv named rather than starting a second session under the same id or, worse, silently attaching and dropping the caller's arguments. The in-flight map therefore stores the argv beside the promise: an identical concurrent launch joins the flight, a differing one chains behind it and meets the same refusal instead of racing a second spawn.

The ONE difference between the two pane surfaces, and the reason cooperative is a separate enum value rather than a flag on embedded (spec 078, F77). Both reserve a Surfaces item and both are passed RENGINE_SURFACE_PORT/RENGINE_SURFACE_TOKEN; only embedded is also handed the adapter on DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES. If a game that connects for itself were ALSO injected, two producers would greet the same token on the same channel; Surfaces.accept keeps the first socket to arrive and destroys the second, and both clients reconnect after a close (the adapter has its own connect loop, the consumer's writer and reader threads retry), so the surviving producer is whichever wins a restart race -- on every reconnect, with no error reported anywhere. Keep this an equality test against 'embedded': widening it to streamsIntoPane() is exactly the edit that recreates the race, and orchestrator/tests/cooperative.test.mjs asserts against it by inspecting the environment this line composes (the child cannot report it -- macOS purges DYLD_* before a protected interpreter starts). The adapter and its macOS-only precondition live with the same equality test in inspectGame above, so a cooperative record is ready on every platform.
